On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya — armed with his sword — confronted Sitaram at the locked door, forced his way past him, disarmed and bound Sitaram to the floor, and left him behind as he escaped the inner quarters. Sitaram was the helpless, tied-up guard left in Udayaditya's wake. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the roles were completely reversed: Sitaram now came to Udayaditya's prison cell, found him lost in despair, declared that the prison was on fire, grabbed him "and almost carried him out," and led him to freedom in the open field where Udayaditya, disoriented and dependent, had to ask Sitaram what to do and where to go — and Sitaram simply told him to follow. The master who had overpowered and bound the guard was now the captive being carried to safety by the very guard he had left tied up on the floor.

Pratapaditya's initial, failed plan was to send two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. This failed because the Pathan Khan Saheb refused to carry out the assassination and instead helped Basanta Ray escape. The method that finally succeeded in ending Basanta Ray's life was a death sentence carried out by beheading—Muktiyar Khan arrived at the fort with soldiers, captured Udayaditya, delivered Pratapaditya's signed order to Basanta Ray, and had Abdul execute him with a drawn sword.
The Mahishi's room as a middle-aged woman (Mother Nikasha); the palace room before the king as Ramai Bhand the jester.

Surma consumed poison secretly prepared by Mangala (disguised Rukmini) over five days with mantras and rituals, delivered through the Mahishi, which caused her death rather than her exile to her father's house.

Pratapaditya married another woman, and Vibha arrived at Chandradwip too late—her husband had already wed someone else, shattering all her hopes of happiness and leaving her utterly alone and heartbroken.

The ring that Rukmini had taken from Udayaditya bore a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name. Sitaram and Bhagavat used this seal to stamp a forged petition alleging that Udayaditya was lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor. Bhagavat then presented this forged petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he had intercepted it from a fleeing servant of Udayaditya. Seeing the Yubaraj's official seal on the document, Pratapaditya flew into a rage and ordered Udayaditya's imprisonment, using the sealed petition as evidence of his supposed treason.

Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape led to Udayaditya freeing the dismissed guards Sitaram and Bhagavat and secretly providing them with monthly stipends. When Pratapaditya learned of these stipends, he was enraged by what he perceived as Udayaditya's defiance and unauthorized mercy. Upon discovering that Surma was actively facilitating the secret continuation of these stipends through her trusted maid, Pratapaditya ordered Surma to be sent to her paternal home—exiling her from the palace as a retaliatory measure against Udayaditya, whom he could not directly punish without risking further conflict. Thus, Surma became the indirect target of Pratapaditya's wrath, a consequence stemming from the chain of events set in motion by Ramchandra Ray's escape.

The song expresses the profound pain of loss, loneliness, and longing — the anguish of those left behind after loved ones and joy have departed. Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, alone on the veranda of his palace in Raigarh at sunset, reflecting personal nostalgia and the quiet sorrow of an old man who has lost his companions and the ability to make music; and second, in the desolate inner quarters of the royal palace in Jessore, after learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, where the song transforms into an expression of collective grief over the devastation of his beloved family and the destruction of all that once brought them joy.

Rukmini's failure to stop Udayaditya's midnight escape allowed him to flee with Basanta Ray. After the escape, Sitaram returned and set fire to Udayaditya's empty prison cell, spreading the rumor that the Yubaraj had died in the flames. When Pratapaditya later learned that Udayaditya had actually escaped — not perished — he summoned Muktiyar Khan and issued a secret death sentence for Basanta Ray, the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan traveled to Raigarh, captured Udayaditya, and then went to Basanta Ray's prayer room to carry out the order. Basanta Ray read the signed decree, recognized Pratapaditya's handwriting, and was executed by Abdul's sword — making Rukmini's failed intervention the direct catalyst that set the entire chain of events leading to Basanta Ray's death.

While Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra with cool indifference—barely acknowledging him, keeping him waiting, accepting his respects without joy or haste, and making him feel clearly subordinate—Ramchandra later reverses this dynamic by constantly mocking and belittling Pratapaditya in his own court, claiming that marrying his daughter has redeemed his family's honor and that Pratapaditya's lineage is insignificant. In short, the one who was first treated as lesser now treats the other as lesser, and the condescension once shown by Pratapaditya toward Ramchandra is returned in full by Ramchandra toward Pratapaditya in his own court.

The Rajmahishi (Pratapaditya's mother), learning that a widow named Mangala (Rukmini) knew various forms of tantra and medicine, sent Matangini to secretly fetch poison from her. Mangala spent five days preparing the poison with mantras and rituals specifically designed so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma died. Surma took this poisoned medicine and died. Subsequently, Rukmini also appeared directly in the palace at night, entering Udayaditya's room while he held Surma's daughter, confronting him and attempting to win his love back, deepening his despair after Surma's death.

Udayaditya's early lament—wishing he had never been born as crown prince and asking what penance could reverse his fate—culminates in Chapter 34 when, brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he formally renounces the throne. After declaring he is not worthy and does not want the kingdom, he swears an oath touching the feet of Ma-Kali: he vows that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of Jessore's kingdom, will not sit on the throne, and will not even touch the royal scepter. If he ever breaks this oath, he declares, may all the sin of his grand-uncle's murder be upon him. He requests to leave for Kashi to live as an ascetic, establish a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name, and designates Samaraditya as the heir to the kingdom.

Nayanchand intercepted the letter by refusing to deliver it to Jessore and giving it to the Mahishi instead; the Mahishi then showed it to Basanta Ray, who misrepresented it as Ramchandra's mere anger and told the household that Ramchandra had written a letter requesting Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house.

Pratapaditya had ordered the canal adjoining the royal palace blocked with large logs of Sal wood, where Ramchandra Ray's sixty-four-oared boat was moored, intending to trap him there. However, Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the blocking logs. The guards, delayed by the need to find a gun (which lacked flintlock and bullets) and then to fetch a chase boat (which was further delayed at a shop), could not intercept in time. By the time the boat reached the Bhairav river and Fernandez fired a cannon, Pratapaditya was startled awake only to find his guards had already fled.

As Basanta Ray's despair over Udayaditya deepens, his relationship with his sitar deteriorates in parallel. In Chapter 13, his playing is visibly hindered by grief — his eyes blur with tears, his throat chokes, and he is forced to stop and set the sitar down; at departure he declares he will leave it behind and never play again. By Chapter 27, the sitar is "no longer with him," and when he finally mentions it, he admits its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned — a physical ruin mirroring the emotional ruin caused by Udayaditya's imprisonment, leaving him unable to create music or find joy, just as he is unable to reach or save the beloved grandson he once sang for.

Udayaditya's willingness to intervene on behalf of his oppressed subjects disappears entirely after Surma's death. Previously, he was known for actively fighting oppression—stopping officials from beating subjects, helping those in need, and acting against the king's wishes to protect his people. After Surma's death, however, a blind fear of Pratapaditya takes hold of him; his former courage vanishes, and he becomes unable to intervene in any situation, no matter how urgent. He turns away from helping instead of stepping forward, hesitates rather than acts, and his compassion for his suffering subjects is completely overridden by paralyzing dread of Pratapaditya's power.

Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape from prison by telling him that a fire has broken out near the palace and grabbing him to lead him to safety, thereby freeing him from the imprisonment that resulted from the forged petition.

In the first desperate occasion (Chapter 11), Rammohan tied together several thick, large sheets to form a rope, secured it to a pillar on the palace roof near the canal, climbed down gripping the rope with his hands and then his teeth, and lowered Ramchandra Ray from the rooftop into the sixty-four-oared boat floating below in the canal, then jumped down himself.

In the second desperate occasion (Chapter 37), Rammohan lifted the unconscious and exhausted Vibha from the hostile palace and placed her into one of the palanquins near the gate, then carried her out to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha was lavishly adorned by the Mahishi—wearing eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a carefully styled coiffure—dressed like a princess preparing to receive her son-in-law with pride and joy. By contrast, when she finally seeks Ramchandra Ray in Chandradwip, she refuses a palanquin, declaring she will go "like a common subject, like a beggar-woman," and steps out dressed as a plain common woman with her veil falling, entering the palace uninvited like any maidservant, utterly humiliated and shamed.
In the bedchamber, the window symbolized his longing and hope for Surma's return; in the prison cell, it symbolized his hope for freedom and liberation.

Sitaram initially frequented Rukmini under the pretense of needing money, using flirtatious banter and false promises to repay loans to extract cash for his household. The dynamic shifted when Udayaditya was imprisoned; Sitaram went to Rukmini to threaten her and vow to free the Yubaraj, but Rukmini revealed that Udayaditya was actually *her* Yubaraj, exposing her own ulterior motives behind her earlier affection. After Sitaram orchestrated the Yubaraj's escape by burning the prison, he visited Rukmini's house to rob her, finding her in a despairing state. This became a life-threatening encounter when Rukmini, enraged and shattered by the loss of her lover, chased Sitaram with a curved blade, forcing him to flee. Their hostility culminated in Rukmini publicly testifying against the plot, demanding severe punishment for the guards involved in the escape.

Sitaram's strategy began with setting fire to the guardhouse huts to create chaos and clear the guards from around Udayaditya's prison, exploiting their customary laxity near the compliant prisoner. Once Udayaditya had escaped, Sitaram escalated the fire into a deliberate cover-up by setting Udayaditya's empty cell itself ablaze — burning the windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and wooden fences — then throwing bones, a skull, and the Yubaraj's sword into the flames to fabricate evidence of death. When guards rushed in after hearing screams, Sitaram falsely declared that the roof had collapsed with no response from the Yubaraj, manufacturing a narrative that the prisoner had perished. He also retrieved and destroyed Udayaditya's letters sent to the palace, eliminating documentary proof. By the time Rukmini attempted to expose the truth at Pratapaditya's assembly, Sitaram had already fled, and the king — either unwilling or unable to acknowledge the conspiracy — remained silent, allowing the fabricated account of the Yubaraj's death in the fire to stand unchallenged.

Ramchandra Ray interprets Udayaditya's protective actions as motivated not by genuine loyalty or heroism, but by self-interest—believing that Udayaditya had saved him primarily for the sake of his own sister, Vibha. He feels that Udayaditya's actions were something that would naturally occur to anyone in that position ("it was bound to happen; for it not to happen would have been wrong"), and that Udayaditya should have foreseen the danger and acted accordingly without needing to be prompted. Because of this mindset, Ramchandra Ray feels no gratitude and instead joins the courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya, viewing him merely as Pratapaditya's son rather than as someone who had risked his life to save the king.

Udayaditya himself authored a forged petition accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor of Delhi, stamped with his own seal, thereby turning the Emperor's authority — the very threat Pratapaditya had repeatedly dismissed — into the instrument used to imprison him.

Surma secretly styles Vibha's hair against the Mahishi's wishes, demonstrating her active presence and close bond with Vibha. Following Surma's tragic absence, Vibha waits for Surma to braid her hair, but Surma never comes, leaving Vibha's hair unbraided and neglected, thus physically marking Surma's departure and Vibha's resulting sorrow.
